cells.tense: Right now you are bearing the weight that has already arrived, and it is not bending you.
cells.ask: Set one load down for an hour where another person can see, and don't rush to lift it again.
cells.core:
The first real weight of something is in your hands and you're carrying it without it carrying you. You can hear when you've started to force it, and you ease off on your own. Things you hold tend to stay whole. That's happening now, whether or not the day shows it.

Keeping this means keeping the trick that makes it work: you hold the form, you don't squeeze it into shape. The strength you've got is a place things can rest a while, not a press. Set one load down for an hour where someone can watch you do it, and let them see you not hurry to take it back. That's how you find out how much of it is yours to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it without crushing it, and that's the whole of it.
cells.verb: Holding the first bare weight of something you intend to make
cells.place: Where the body carries what has to be carried until the thing can stand on its own

cells.tense: You are already bracing for the weight that hasn't come yet, holding a load no one has handed you.
cells.ask: Leave one person's problem with them for the day and don't check whether it landed.
cells.core:
You're holding things before they arrive. Someone hasn't asked and you've already taken their shape, standing ready with strength they didn't request. The bracing is real work, spent on nothing that exists yet.

When you carry only what's actually in front of you, your strength stays usable for the day in front of you. You hold your own load and the people around you hold theirs. Put one person's problem down and let it stay with them. Not forget it. Just leave it where it is and don't check on it. What comes back when you stop pre-carrying is the feel of your own weight, the real one.

cells.tense: The weight was there and the hands carrying it stopped, and you're still standing where the carrying used to happen.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been not-carrying, out loud to someone, and stay for the answer you get.
cells.core:
Something came along and you didn't pick it up. Not refused it — didn't reach. What's left is a strange steadiness, like the body learned to hold still instead of hold up. You have endurance. You're just not spending it on anything, and the space where the weight would be is louder than the weight ever was.

What's out of reach isn't the strength; it's seeing one thing clearly enough to take it. Choose one thing you've been not-carrying and say it out loud to someone. Don't lift it while you say it. Say it and stay in the room for whatever comes back.
cells.sheetLine: You have the strength. You just stopped spending it.

cells.tense: You are holding up more than you've said you're holding, and you call it a normal amount.
cells.ask: Say 'I'm carrying this' about one load you've been calling ordinary, to someone who can hear it, today.
cells.core:
Look at the load you're under and the words you use for it. You say the day is normal. You say this is what carrying looks like. But someone in your life is standing on what you're holding for them, and you haven't said that it's yours. The bearing is working. The saying-so isn't.

What's absent isn't strength. It's telling it once, plainly, about one load you've been calling ordinary. That's not admitting weakness. It's calling the load by its real name so the one carrying it can be seen. Say it once, to a person who can take it, and let the sentence be enough.
cells.sheetLine: You hold more than you say. Tell it once, plainly.
